scenarioName: Pediatric Fall from Height — The Quiet Child, Compensated Shock, and Scene-Time Discipline

scenarioStory.history: 6-year-old boy who fell roughly 10 feet from the upper platform of a playground climbing structure onto packed dirt and wood chips, landing directly on his left side. The fall was witnessed by the playground supervisor. He did not lose consciousness — he sat up on his own — but he has not cried, has not called for anyone, and has not spoken since. He is sitting propped against the base of the structure, leaning back, staring at nothing. When the supervisor asked if he was okay he did not answer. He is guarding his left upper abdomen and pulls away when it is touched. The supervisor, who has run this playground for eleven years, says: 'They always cry. Every single one of them cries. He hasn't made a sound.' His skin is pale and cool. There is no external bleeding, no obvious deformity, and no head wound.
scenarioStory.course: Initial Contact: A 6-year-old, 20 kg, ten-foot fall onto his left side, and his blood pressure is 98/58 — which is NORMAL for his age. That number is the trap, and it will kill him if the crew believes it. MATC's pediatric hypotension threshold for a 6-year-old is 70 + (2 × 6) = 82 mmHg systolic. He is above it, and he is in profound shock anyway. Children are compensatory masters: they clamp down peripherally and run their heart rate up, holding a normal pressure until they have lost a devastating fraction of their blood volume, and then they do not fade — they fall off a cliff. MATC states this outright in the trauma guideline's safety considerations: patients with compensated shock may not manifest hypotension until severe blood loss has occurred. Everything else on this child is screaming. Heart rate 148. Capillary refill 4 seconds. Pale, cool skin. Left upper quadrant guarding after a direct left-side impact — a splenic injury until proven otherwise. And the silence. A 6-year-old who falls ten feet and does not cry is not brave and is not stoic; he is not perfusing his brain. The protocol answer is not complicated and it is not slow: MARCH, 20 mL/kg of crystalloid, scene time under ten minutes, and drive to the trauma center. → Load and go; bolus en route: Packaged and rolling in eight minutes. The 400 mL bolus is running through a line established in the back of a moving ambulance, because the protocol says explicitly not to delay transport to obtain IV access — and if the line had been difficult, the answer was an IO, not a longer scene time. He responds the way a compensating child responds: the heart rate comes down from 148 to 132, capillary refill improves to 3 seconds, and he mumbles a one-word answer when asked his name. That is real improvement, and it is also completely misleading. He is still bleeding into his abdomen. Crystalloid replaces volume; it does not replace blood, and it does not close a lacerated spleen. The destination decision is the one that matters now, and MATC does not leave it to taste: transport to the highest level of care within the trauma system, per the ACS-COT field triage guideline. The community hospital five minutes away has no pediatric surgeon. Twenty minutes to a Level 1 pediatric trauma center is the correct answer even though it is the longer drive, because the thing this child needs is an operating room, and only one of those two buildings has the right one.

relatedChecklist: MARCH primary survey: Massive hemorrhage, Airway, Respiratory, Circulation, Head/Hypothermia
Recognize COMPENSATED shock — a normal BP does not exclude severe blood loss in a child
400 mL crystalloid bolus IV/IO (20 kg × 20 mL/kg); reassess; repeat for persistent shock
Scene time UNDER 10 MINUTES — he needs a surgeon, and you are not one
Spinal motion restriction — fall >10 ft AND abnormal mental status both trigger it
Supplemental oxygen to maintain SpO2 >94%; support ventilation if needed
Prevent hypothermia — 52°F ambient, small child, shock; remove wet clothing and cover him
Maintain SBP >82 mmHg (70 + 2×6 yrs) — prevent hypotension, do not wait for it
Consider TXA — within 3 hours of injury with signs of hemorrhagic shock

scenarioEvents.name: Stayed on scene; reassured by normal BP
scenarioEvents.description: The crew did a thorough job on that playground. A complete head-to-toe. Two careful IV attempts in a child with no visible veins. A splint for a wrist that was never broken. A conversation about whether to wait for the parents. Twelve minutes in, the blood pressure was still 'normal,' and that was the number they kept coming back to. At the ten-minute mark he stopped compensating. Children do not decline gradually — they hold the line, and hold it, and hold it, and then the line breaks all at once. His pressure fell from 98 to 66 systolic in under two minutes. Radial pulses are gone. His skin is mottled. His heart rate spiked to 172 and has now begun to FALL toward 44, which in a bleeding child is not a rhythm problem — it is the agonal bradycardia of a heart with nothing left to pump. He is minutes from a traumatic arrest on a playground twenty minutes from the only surgeon who could have saved him. The lesson is exactly the one the protocol wrote down: patients with compensated shock may not manifest hypotension until severe blood loss has occurred. The blood pressure was never a measure of how he was doing. It was a measure of how long he could keep pretending.
relatedChecklist: Manage the airway; BVM at 20 breaths/min (age 2–14) with gentle volumes — chest rise only
LOAD NOW and resuscitate en route — he needs an operating room, not a better playground
400 mL boluses (20 mL/kg) repeated; target a palpable radial pulse; 1200 mL total → medical direction
IO access now — tibial site preferred in children; stop trying for a peripheral vein
Aggressively warm him — cold + acidotic + bleeding is the coagulopathy spiral
Debrief: a normal BP in a tachycardic, poorly perfused child is the WARNING, not the reassurance
